title: Polymeric-PVAc/Pd hybrid nanoparticles to enhance the electrochemical performance of graphene supercapacitors and their role to accelerate the photodegradation of methylene blue dye
abstract: Abstract We report the utilization of SiO 2 /VO x /MnO x /SiC (SVMG) microparticles, palladium nanoparticles (Pd-NPs), and polymeric nanoparticles (P-NPs) made of poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) to enhance the energy density/capacitance of flexible supercapacitors (SCs). For this, the SVMG + P@Pd composite was incorporated onto graphene (Gph) electrodes printed on recycled plastic substrates. SCs fabricated with SVMG + P@Pd composite reached a capacitance of 828.3 F g −1  and energy density of 115.03 Wh kg −1 . This performance was 93% superior compared to a reference SC fabricated without the SVMG + P@Pd composite (made only with Gph electrodes). SCs made with SVMG + P@Pd composite demonstrated a superior electrochemical performance compared with SCs fabricated with SVMG (492.90 F g −1 , 68.45 Wh kg −1 ), SVMG + Pd-NPs (507.74 F g −1 , 70.52 Wh kg −1 ) and P-NPs + Pd-NPs composite (432.21 F g −1 , 65.78 Wh kg −1 ). XPS analysis revealed the rich presence of oxygen vacancies and redox activity of species such as Si 2+ /Si 3+ /Si 4+ , Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ /Mn 4+ , V 3+ /V 4+ /V 5+ , and Pd 2+ /Pd 4+ , which acted as the primary redox centers for energy storage. Additionally, SVMG + P@Pd composite was evaluated for the photocatalytic degradation of methylene blue (MB) dissolved in drinking water. Such composite degraded 89% of MB after 30 min under sunlight. Furthermore, photocatalytic floaters made without P-NPs or without P@Pd removed a maximum of 85% for MB. From scavenger experiments, we found that holes (h + ) were the main oxidizing species, while •O 2 −  and •OH radicals were the secondary oxidizing species. Adding Polymeric + Pd nanoparticles to SVMG microparticles increased the content of oxygen vacancies, which not only serves to store charge in SCs but also delays the recombination of photogenerated charges, increasing the photodegradation of MB.
journal: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Electronics

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: From health monitoring systems and fitness trackers to various interactive electronic devices (smartwatches and reality glasses), wearable electronics have boomed in recent years, becoming essential in personal applications and revolutionizing technology/user interaction [ 1 ]. However, integrating such devices into daily-life applications requires compact and flexible energy storage systems (ESS) that can efficiently provide reliable high performance. To date, flexible Li-ion batteries (fLIBs) are the main ESS because they are known to store huge amount of energy as compared with other types of electrochemical energy storage devices, including supercapacitors (SCs) [ 2 ]. Nevertheless, fLIBs are also known to possess low power delivery/uptake, short cycle life and thermal management issues, thus, alternatives with high power and high energy densities are needed [ 3 ]. On the other hand, SCs have gained increasing attention in the scientific field, especially because they can be fully charged and discharged in seconds, resulting in much higher power delivery/uptake that can be achieved in shorter times. Also, SCs are used due to other distinct characteristics features, such as better stability for the continuous cycling, low cost, environmental friendliness, and safety [ 3 ]. Since electrodes are the heart of supercapacitors with respect to their energy storage performance, developing novel high capacitance electrode materials capable of providing more active sites (oxygen vacancies, redox species, etc.) during the electrochemical reaction process is one of the most effective strategies to improve the energy density of SCs. Recently, many studies in the field of SCs have proved that incorporating these active sites into a conductive network produces a synergistic effect that further enhance SCs performance [ 4 ].

Among a wide variety of electrode materials for SCs, graphene (Gph) highlights as one of the high performance choice due to its large theoretical specific surface are of 2630 m 2  g −1 , outstanding electrical conductivity close to 10 7  S m −1 , highly stable physico-chemical properties and great flexibility [ 5 ]. In addition, the results of different scientific investigations have shown that the theoretical capacitance of a single layer of Gph can reach values up to 550 F g −1  when the full surface area is able to be utilized [ 6 ]. Therefore, Gph is one of the most cited materials introduced recently in SC devices, resulting in an electrochemical performance with metrics of capacitance in the range of 100–320 F g −1  and maximum energy density near to 40 Wh kg −1  [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ]. Such performance values in the Gph-based SCs may not necessarily meet the desired energy storage specifications in applications requiring high energy density. To alleviate this problem, the strategy for introducing inorganic and/or organic nanocomposites with high redox activity and excellent conductivity in the Gph electrode is considered to be one of the most promising methods. Among them, composites based on silicon carbide (SiC) are well known to have large surface areas for high energy densities and in combination with different metal oxides containing multiple valence states exhibit high redox activity, which can provide additional storage of charge by redox activity. For example, Wu et al. [ 10 ] achieved excellent electrochemical results from a SC device by including electrodes of SiC and MnCo 2 O 4  composite. In fact, this device produced an energy density of 90.3 Wh kg −1  together with 92.1% capacitance retention after 10,000 charge/discharge (C/D) cycles. Additionally, Asghar et al. [ 11 ] reported the fabrication of a SiOC/Bi 2 O 3  nanocomposite for SC. When using this nanocomposite as electrode material, the SC showed capacitance of 500 F g −1 , energy density of 98.2 Wh kg −1 , and capacitance retention (after 5,000 C/D cycles) of 95.55%. Zhang et al. [ 12 ] intercalated the SiOC into a Gph-based hybrid membrane and used it as electrode material for the fabrication of a SC due to its enhance electrolyte transport and high synergy between Gph and SiOC. Hence, the resulting device demonstrated electrochemical performance with capacitance and energy density values of 211 F g −1  and 86.8 Wh kg −1 , respectively. Also, this SC retained 98.2% of its initial capacitance after 10,000 C/D cycles. Furthermore, the group of Gao et al. [ 13 ] manufactured ternary composite electrodes by including the following components: N, S co-doped SiOC, nickel oxide and nickel cobaltate. Using these electrodes, the constructed SC reached capacitance of 254.5 F g −1 , energy density of 66.9 Wh kg −1  and only lost 22.7% of its original capacitance after 5,000 C/D cycles. However, SCs have some limitations. For example, the demonstration of high energy density results together with the complexity of the synthesized materials and structures. Another strategy to boost the electrochemical performance of SCs consists in including polymer nanoparticles in their fabrication. This is primary due to the high electrical conductivity, flexibility, and cost-effectiveness of conducting polymers [ 14 ]. In recent literature, the use of conducting polymer nanoparticles in the fabrication of SCs has produced the following electrochemical performance results: Shinde et al. [ 15 ] reported capacitance of 406 F g −1 , energy density of 60.60 Wh kg −1  and capacitance retention of 94% after 5000 C/D cycles from a SC device fabricated by coating polyaniline (PANI) on NiCo 2 O 4  porous nanoflakes at the SC electrodes; Luo et al. [ 16 ] introduced polypyrrole (PPy) together with Ti 3 C 2 T x  MXene as composite electrode for the fabrication of SCs, which display capacitance of 130 F g −1 , energy density of 35.3 Wh kg −1  and its capacitance attenuation was 13.2% after 6,000 C/D cycles; Ma et al. [ 17 ] prepared poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS) electrodes functionalized with Ti 3 C 2 T x  MXene. Based on these electrodes, the constructed SCs showed capacitance, energy density, and capacitance retention values of 293 F g −1 , 56.34 Wh kg −1 , and 75% at 5 k C/D cycles; Zainul et al. [ 18 ] grew MCo 2 O 4  nanospheres on graphitic carbon nitride/PPy nanoparticles and the electrochemical evaluation of this material as electrode inside an SC produced capacitance and energy density values of 350 F g −1  and 70 Wh kg −1 . Also, this device was capable of retain 94.55% of its initial capacitance after 5,000 C/D cycles. On the other hand, even when the high cost and finite reserves of Pd restricts its massive application, it is well known that this noble metal has great potential in a wide variety of applications, including the fabrication of SCs with good electrochemical performance. For example, Ahangari et al. [ 19 ] reported the partial substitution of Pd in B site of the La 0.8 Sr 0.2 Cu 0.7 Mn 0.3 O 3  perovskite oxide and the further use of this material in the fabrication of a SC, which displayed capacitance and energy density values of 113 F g −1  and 63.3 Wh kg −1 , respectively. Also, recent literature has elucidated the use of Pd to enhance the photocatalytic activity to degrade different organic pollutants with efficiency results above 95% in less than 2 h. For instance, Ghadage et al. [ 20 ] degraded malachite green dye (MG), Deng et al. [ 21 ] degraded tetracycline, and Al-nayili et al. [ 22 ] degraded Rhodamine B (RhB). In particular, the previously collected literature demonstrates that electrodes containing two or more components are applied in high performance SCs due to their synergistic effects.

With the aim to demonstrate that a SiC-based compound can be used together with polymeric and Pd nanoparticles (P- and Pd-NPs) for energy storage, in this work, we proposed the fabrication of a flexible SC device by including in its electrodes the following components: i) a synthesized SiO 2 /VO x /MnO x /SiC (SVMG) powder and ii) polymeric nanoparticles (P-NPs) made of poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) colloidally stabilized with poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) and iii) Pd-NPs. First, Gph layer was printed on recycled polypropylene (PP) substrates to form graphene electrode. Later SVMG, P-NPs, and Pd-NPs were deposited on the graphene electrodes. The resulting device was labeled as SVMG + P@Pd-SC and it exhibited outstanding capacitance and energy density values of 828.23 F g −1  and 115.03 Wh kg 1 , respectively. Such performance results were superior in comparison with other ones obtained from a series of devices also fabricated in this investigation. For example, the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device made with SVMG, polymeric nanoparticles, and Pd nanoparticles exhibited 93.3, 68.04, and 63.1% superior performance than the devices fabricated with electrodes containing only pure Gph layers (Gph-SC), SVMG compound (SVMG-SC), or Pd nanoparticles, respectively. These last findings indicate that the addition of each component until the formation of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrodes (made of SVMG + Polymeric-NPs + Pd-NPs), the SC system gradually increments its energy storage capacity since the synergy between each component and the Gph template increments the presence of different oxidation states, allowing rich storage of charge via redox mechanism. Furthermore, the structure of the SVMG + P@Pd-E resulted to be highly stable by retaining 92% and 93.5% of its initial capacitance after the application of cycling stability tests (1,000 bending cycles and 1,000 C/D cycles). In addition, the same SVMG + P@Pd-E composite electrode was used as photocatalytic floater for the degradation of methylene blue (MB) under natural solar light (a sustainable energy source). By using the SVMG + P@Pd photocatalyst (SVMG + P@Pd–PT), the degradation of MB successfully reached 89% efficiency after only 30 min of photocatalytic reaction. This outstanding photodegradation performance by the SVMG + P@Pd composite was primary attributed to the synergy between all the components in the ternary composite. For reference, SVMG photocatalyst powders reached degradation efficiencies (under the same photodegradation conditions) of 84%, respectively. The enhancement occurred because decorating the SVMG material win P- and Pd-NPs induced higher separation of charges and enhanced the photocatalytic activity. Overall, the key innovations of this research are as follows: i) It is demonstrated that Polymeric-PVAc@Pd hybrid nanoparticles can be deposited on metal oxides to enhance their capacitance and photocatalytic activity; ii) the synthesis of the SVMG powder and its application as redox component in SC electrodes, which has not been investigated in previous publications; iii) obtaining an energy density of 115.03 Wh kg −1 , being the highest reported so far for SCs made with Pd, SiC, or polymeric nanoparticles; and iv) the fast degradation of MB (89% after only 30 min) produced by the SVMG + Polymeric-NPs + Pd-NPs (SVMG + P@Pd) composite under sunlight. All the results of this study emphasize the potential of the novel SVMG + P@Pd hybrid composites to be a multifunctional material capable of energy storage and can be used for environmental remediation.

sections.heading: Chemicals
paragraphs: Tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS, 98%), Pluronic F-127, NH 4 VO 3  (99%), Mn(NO3)2 (98%), Vinyl acetate (Vac; monomer), ammonium persulfate (APS; initiator), and PVA (surfactants) were all purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Graphene microflakes were purchased from American materials Corporation.

sections.heading: Synthesis of SVMG compound and polymeric nanoparticles
paragraphs: SiO 2 /VO x /MnO x /G/SiC (SVMG) powder was prepared through the sol/gel process, in which a precursor solution of tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) was used on the hydrolysis and polycondensation reaction [ 23 ]. Briefly, TEOS was added drop by drop to a mixture solution made with 50 ml of ethanol, 0.5 g of Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), and 20 ml of distilled water (solution A). After stirring for 60 min, the pH was set to 5.0 using a 1 M HCl solution. Then, two solutions were prepared, solution B with Pluronic F-127 surfactant, ethanol (20 ml), NH 4 VO 3  and Mn(NO 3 ) 2 ; solution C was prepared with SiC, ethanol (20 ml), and PVP. Afterward, a final solution was prepared by mixing and stirring at 85 °C these three solutions A, B, and C. Finally, after this final solution was cool down at 25 °C and then washed with hexanes and ethanol, the resulting powder was named SVMG which was finally dried at 80 °C for 30 min. Polymeric nanoparticles (P-NPs) were synthesized by emulsion polymerization of vinyl acetate at 60 °C in a batch reactor, using ammonium persulfate as the initiator and PVA as the surfactant. The latter has a degree of hydrolysis of 87–89% and a nominal molar mass of 13,000–23,000 Da. For further details on the synthesis of the Polymeric-NPs, see the article reported by Olvera-Guillén et al. [ 24 ].

sections.heading: Electrode’s preparation and SC assembling
paragraphs: To fabricate the solid-state SCs, filter paper was dipped in PVA/H 3 PO 4  gel electrolyte solution (PVA/distilled water/H 3 PO 4 ) to be used both as separator and as electrolyte. First, a symmetric SC was fabricated by sandwiching two flexible Gph electrodes separated by the PVA/H 3 PO 4  filter paper. Then, the two-electrode cell designated as Gph-SC was packaged with a transparent polymer film after heat-sealing process and the prepared device served as reference. Following the same procedure, another device was assembled by sandwiching two SVMG-E electrodes, forming a symmetric SC labeled as SVMG-SC. On the other hand, other symmetric SCs were SVMG + P-SC (contained SVMG + P-NPs), SVMG + P@Pd-SC (contained SVMG + P-Nps + Pd-NPs), and Gph + P@Pd-E-SC (contained P-NPs + Pd-NPs).

sections.heading: Materials characterization
paragraphs: Scanning electron (SEM, Quanta 250) and transmission electron (TEM, FEI Talos F200S) microscopes were used to acquire high-resolution images of the material’s morphology. Meanwhile, material’s elemental composition was studied with an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) fitted to SEM. For X-ray diffraction measurements (XRD) of the materials, a diffractometer (Bruker D8 advanced) using iron-filtered Cu Kα radiation in the 2θ range of 10°–80° was applied. Fourier transform infrared spectra (FTIR) in the energy range of 400–4000 cm −1  were collected on a Shimadzu spectrometer with attenuated total reflectance (ATR) sampling. Furthermore, UV–visible (UV–Vis) absorbance measurements, Raman spectra, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) examinations were applied on the prepared electrodes in order to reveal their energy storage mechanism. For UV–Vis measurements in the range of 200–800 nm, a spectrophotometer Carry 500 was employed. Raman spectroscopic measurements in the shift range of 2000–1000 cm −1  were performed on Renishaw inVia micro-Raman microscope, which had a 532 nm laser. For XPS analysis, a Thermo-Fisher-Scientific K alpha instrument equipped with a monochromatic Al K source was utilized.

sections.heading: Electrochemical characterization
paragraphs: To evaluate the capacitance, energy density, and power density of SCs accurately, each electrochemical test was repeated five times under the same conditions and applied to five different SCs.

sections.heading: Photocatalytic tests
Studies of morphology, crystallinity, and chemical bonding at the surface of the prepared electrodes
paragraphs: Figure  1 a shows the electron micrograph of the SVMG-E, revealing the coalescence of the SVMG powders between the cracks of the Gph layers, as marked in the region of the red dashed rectangle. The fractures on the Gph layer were formed as the result of the overlapping among the graphene microflakes with average surface of 80–120 µm 2 . Fig. 1 Scanning electron micrographs of  a  SVMG-E,  b  SVMG@Pd-E and  c  SVMG + P@Pd-E electrodes.  d  EDS spectrum of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode. Inset in Fig. 1a displays a SEM micrograph of the SVMG powders. Inset of Fig. 1c shows a closer view of the particles in the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode

Also, in the inset of Fig.  1 a, the SVMG powder was observed to exhibit distinct morphology of cage-like aggregated structure. This physical combination between both Gph and SVMG is beneficial as it allows the pseudocapacitive process of charge storage to occur more effectively through the Gph layer, enhancing the whole process of transport, extraction, and charge storage across the electrode. Figure  1 b displays the electron micrograph of the SVMG@Pd-E electrode, which exhibits the SVMG powder covered by the Pd-NPs while supported on the Gph layers. In order to present a better visualization of the Pd-NPs, Figure  S1 (a-b) of the supporting information depicts the image corresponding to the performed TEM analysis. Both imagens, which were obtained at different magnifications, clearly show a consistent pattern of small, uniform, and narrowly distributed spherical Pd-NPs with diameters falling within the range of 10 to 12 nm. This cause that some areas of the electrode present a higher density of tiny Pd-NPs covering the SVMG microparticles (indicated by the orange dashed circles), whereas other regions showed a more dispersed presence of the SVMG@Pd compound (highlighted by the blue dashed circles). Rather than being detrimental, this heterogeneity is advantageous as it allows the direct contact at the Gph/electrolyte interface, increasing the contact area with the composite particles and in consequence enhancing ion/charge storage diffusion. Additionally, the electron micrograph of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode is shown in Fig.  1 c. From here, highlights the presence of the spherical P-NPs together with the Pd-NPs anchored to the SVMG. An amplified view of the Pd-NPs in the inset of Fig.  1 c clearly shows its well-defined spherical shape and reveals micrometric diameters in the range of 5 ± 2 µm. The integration of all the components fully covers the entire Gph support, which is a valuable insight since this can enhance the availability of reactive sites on the entire surface of the electrode, thereby facilitating an improvement in the pseudocapacitive process for energy storage. On the other side, Fig.  1 d depicts the EDS spectrum of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode, revealing the following elements: C and O from the organic nature components (Gr and Poly); Si, V, and Mn from SVMG; and Pd from the deposited Pd-NPs. Then, the exclusive presence of the materials composing the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode fabrication was confirmed. Moreover, XRD analyses were carried out on the supercapacitor electrodes and for the SVMG powder in order to determine their crystalline structure. Figure  2  presents the diffractograms of the SVMG powder (i), SVMG@Pd-E electrode (ii), and SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode (iii). Fig. 2 X-ray diffraction patterns for the SVMG powder, Gph-E, and SVMG + P@Pd-E electrodes

In order to identify the nature of the chemical bonds on the materials composing the SC electrodes, FTIR analysis was applied first, on the SVMG powder and then on the Gph-E electrode and SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode before and after its use in the SC, as presented in Fig.  3 . Fig. 3 FTIR spectra forthe SVMG powder, Gph-E electrode, and SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode used and not used in the SC

The red spectrum corresponds to the SVMG powder and it displays strong vibrational bands corresponding to the SiC matrix at around 560 cm −1  (Si–O bending), 800 cm −1  (Si–C), 960 cm −1  (Si–OH), and 1050 cm −1  (Si–O) [ 37 ,  38 – 39 ]. Additionally, the spectrum of the SVMG powder also exhibited bands related to the M–O bond due to the presence of the metallic dopants (Mn and V) in the SVMG and to the C = O bond at around 443 and 1650 cm −1 , respectively [ 40 ,  41 ]. Excepting the band at 560 cm −1 , all the bands in the red spectrum were again observed in the FTIR spectrum of the SVMG + P@Pd-E, along with different transmittance bands derived from the presence of the Gph support. The band at 1737 cm −1  corresponds to C = O stretching vibrations, while the band at 2334 cm −1  is attributed to the vibration of CO 2  molecules, which were absorbed on the surface of the electrodes during fabrication in air [ 42 ,  43 ]. As it can be seen by comparing the FTIR spectrum of the Gph-E (black curve) and SVMG + P@Pd-E (blue curve) electrodes, both also share the presence of a transmittance band at 2937 cm −1  associated to the stretching vibration of C-H [ 41 ]. This is because of the presence of the recycled plastic substrate over which both electrodes were fabricated. Furthermore, bands associated with the constituents (PVAc and PVA) of the Pd-NPs were evident on the blue spectrum. The bands at 1425 and 3327 cm −1  correspond to CH 2 -Cl angular deformation and the OH vibration, respectively [ 44 ]. Finally, the load of the Pd-NPs onto the surface of the SVMG + P@Pd-E was indicated by the band at 556 cm −1  [ 45 ]. This finding corroborates the presence of the P-NPs, which promote high electroconductivity and surface redox activity of the additional components included in the fabrication of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode. Following the extraction of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode from the electrochemically tested supercapacitor, the FTIR spectrum of this used electrode (green curve) depicted bands related to chemical bonds between C, H, and O elements. Specifically, bands at 1630 cm −1  (C = O stretching vibration), at 2327 cm −1  (-OH stretching), between 2570 and 3000 cm −1  (C-H bond), and between 3000 and 3650 cm −1  (OH stretching vibration) [ 44 ,  46 ,  47 – 48 ]. Additionally, a band associated to the symmetric stretching of P-O was visible at around 970 cm −1  [ 47 ]. Thus, those vibrational bands demonstrated the formation of different organic groups as defects on the surface of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode, which were derived from the presence of the aqueous PVA/H 3 PO 4  electrolyte after electrochemical test. Such groups are important since they can act as redox centers for the charge storage.

sections.heading: Electrochemical performance of supercapacitors
paragraphs: First, the capacitive performance of SC systems was evaluated by CV measurements. Figure  4 a displays the CVs of the Gph-SC device at different scan rates (25, 50, 75, and 100 mV s −1 ) in the voltage window of 0 – 1.2 V. The nearly rectangular shaped CV curves without redox peaks signifies EDL capacitance characteristics, which stores charge via reversible ion adsorption at the electrode–electrolyte interface. Also, these CVs have a light deviation from typical rectangular shape, indicating good compatibility between electrolyte and electrodes in terms of high ionic conductivity. Figure  4 b shows the CVs obtained from the SVMG-SC, which reveal a profile with redox bands, see the dark dashed circles. With increasing the scanning rates at the same voltage window (0–1.2 V), the area under the CVs increases and the redox peaks move slightly toward both ends of the potential, showing excellent redox reversibility of the SVMG-E electrode. Fig. 4 CVs for the  a  Gph-SC,  b  SVMG-SC,  c  SVMG@Pd-SC, and SVMG + P@Pd-SC devices

Also, Fig.  4 c illustrates the CVs of the SVMG@Pd-SC device. Each CV recorded at the same scanning speeds exhibits a distinguishable redox peak indicated by the dark dashed circle, suggesting the redox behavior of the SVMG@Pd-E electrode. Furthermore, Fig.  4 d presents the CVs of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device, highlighting the prominent redox peaks indicated by the dark dashed circles. According to all the plots of Fig.  4 , when the scan rate increased, the current density of the electrodes also increases, indicating the diffusion process as the main mechanism of charge transfer kinetics. Also, Fig.  4 d shows that the CV curve of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device is 15% wider than the CV curve in Fig.  4 b and approximately 73% wider than the CV in Fig.  4 c, suggesting that the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device provides a superior capacitive storage. In addition, the electrochemical performance of the same four devices was further evaluated by GCD measurements. Figure  5 a illustrates the GCDs for each device at a charging current of 1 A g −1 . Furthermore, a photograph taken from the fabricated device is displayed in the inset of Fig. 5a. Fig. 5 a  GCDs of the Gph-SC, SVMG-SC, SVMG@Pd-SC, and SVMG + P@Pd-SC devices.  B  Capacitance retention plots of SVMG@Pd -SC and SVMG + P@Pd-SC devices after the application of 1000 charge/discharge cycles.  c  CVs and  d  GCDs of the SVMG@Pd-SC devices subjected to 500 bending cycles. Inset in Fig. 5a displays a digital photograph of the SC device

A comparison of these curves indicates that after the first section of the GCDs, where the output voltage gradually declines until the fourth–sixth hour of discharge, the following outcomes can be obtained: (i) the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device has the highest energy storage capacity, as evident by its extended discharge time in the second section of the GCDs, where the voltage stabilizes and remains constant, and (ii) with the addition of each pseudocapacitive component (SVMG, P-NPs, and Pd-NPs) on the Gph electrodes, the output voltage gradually increases until a value of 0.36 V, which is supply by the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device. Furthermore, the GCD technique accompanied with the Eqs. 1 and 2 of Sect.  2.5  is a highly reliable method to analyze/calculate the capacitive and energy density properties of the fabricated SCs. Among all, the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device exhibited the highest capacitance (828.3 F g −1 ) and energy density (115.03 Wh kg −1 ) at power density of 16.37 W kg −1 , followed by the SVMG@Pd-SC device (507.74 F g −1 , 70.52 Wh kg −1  at 10.04 W kg −1 ) and then the SVMG-SC (492.90 F g −1 , 68.45 Wh kg −1  at 9.74 W kg −1 ). From those last results, we infer that devices made with SVMG + Pd-NPs are more capacitive than these containing only SVMG redox powder in their electrodes. Furthermore, the individual contribution of the Pd-NPs toward the overall electrochemical performance of the SC was studied by fabricating SCs whose electrodes contained only Pd-NPs (deposited on graphene electrodes). The CVs and GCD curves of this device (named as Gph + Pd-SC) are shown in Figure S2a and S2b in supporting information, respectively. From here, the CV curves for the Gph + Pd-SC device did not exhibit redox peaks, indicating that the pure Pd-NPs deposited on the electrodes do not produce significant redox reactions. Capacitance and energy density values were obtained from GCD curves in S2b and obtained values of 336.43 F g −1  and 40.61 Wh kg −1 , respectively. Compared with the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device, the devices made only with SVMG or Pd-NPs have lower capacitances of 40–60%. Thus, adding the P-NPs is critical because they added more pores, which facilitated the ion diffusion/extraction, which in turn, benefited the overall capacitance of the devices. In comparison with another reference device (Gph-SC), which delivered capacitance of 428.47 F g −1  and energy density of 59.51 Wh kg −1 , the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device had a 93% higher capacitance and energy density, indicating that the combination of three components (SVMG, P-, and Pd-NPs) drastically enhanced the redox activity. The reasons for which an enhancement of capacitance occurred in the SCs made with the SVMG + P@Pd composite electrodes compared with the one made only with graphene electrodes are the following: i) First, H +  and PO 4 3−  ions move easily through the SVMG + P@Pd composite material due to the porous layer formed by the polymer (as depicted in the SEM of Fig.  1 c), which generates a higher impregnation of the PVA/H 3 PO 4  electrolyte into the SC electrode; consequently, the interaction between the electrolyte ions and the SVMG + Pd-NPs (redox powders) is increased and this promotes higher redox activity for charge storage; and (ii) there is a synergy between the composite material and graphene, which facilitates the extraction of charge to supply energy. Particularly, the redox reactions are absent in the SC made only with Gph electrodes (those ones store charge by electron double-layer mechanism) and extra electrons cannot be generated by redox reactions for charge storage. To better understand the impact of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode in the performance of the SC, CV and GCD measurements were obtained from the Gph + P@Pd-SC device and the results are displayed in Figure S3a and S3b, respectively. As shown, the CVs denoted weak redox activity, resulting from the absence of SVMG powders in the working electrode, while the GCD at 20 mA exhibited higher output voltage (0.19 V) than the reference device, but lower than the other remaining SCs. As a result, the Gph + P@Pd-SC device reached capacitance and energy density values of 432.21 F g −1  and 65.78 Wh kg −1 , respectively. This indicates that excluding the presence of SVMG in the fabrication of the ternary nanocomposite electrode decreases the whole electrochemical performance of the SC by 82%. On the other hand, the cycling stability of the best SVMG + P@Pd-SC device (which had the highest capacitance) was assessed and compared with that one obtained for the device made without polymeric nanoparticles (SVMG@Pd-SC device). As shown in Fig. 5b, the cycling performance results clearly demonstrate that the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device exhibits better cycling stability than the SVMG@Pd-SC device; after 1000 C/D cycles, the percentage of retention of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device was 93.5%, whereas the SVMG@Pd-SC device only retained 86% of its original capacitance. This reflects a superior level of electrochemical stability for the SVMG + P@Pd-E device, which has been produced by the combined redox activity of the SVMG and Pd components. Also, the presence of P-NPs favored the formation of a porous network (see SEM images), that facilitated ion diffusion/extraction in SC electrodes (contained graphene). Afterward, the flexibility of SVMG + P@Pd-SC and SVMG@Pd-SC devices was investigated via application of CV and GCD tests operated at 100 cycles of 0–180 bending with 100 mV s −1  and repeated 5 times. For the SVMG@Pd-SC device, the outputs of the test are displayed in Fig.  5 c, d, along with an inset that exhibits a photograph of the bent device. The five CVs of each 100 bent (see Fig.  5 c) clearly show similar shape to the originals obtained at unbent state, even with the presence of the strong redox peak indicated by the dark dashed circle and without any visible deformation as the bent cycles increased. This result was complemented with the high stability of each of the five GCDs at 100 bents, as shown in Fig.  5 d. In fact, between the fifth GCD and the unbent GCD (see blue curve of Fig.  5 a), there was only a difference of 0.03 V in the supply voltage of the SVMG@Pd-SC device. Similarly, Fig.  6 a, b illustrates that the CVs and GCDs of the 500 times bent SVMG + P@Pd-SC device have a great stability in shape and supply voltage, respectively. Fig. 6 a  CVs and  b  GCDs of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device exposed to 1000 bending cycles.  c  Capacitance retention plots of the SVMG@Pd-SC and SVMG + P@Pd-SC devices after the application of 1000 bending cycles. Inset inFig. 6b displays a digital photograph of the SC devic

In this case, the operating voltage from the GCD curves corresponding to devices subjected to 500 bending cycles showed a value that was 25% lower compared with that obtained from the same device before the application of the bending cycles. From here, it is conceivable that the flexible stability of both devices could continue with further cycling. In fact, Fig.  6 c demonstrates the exceptional long-term mechanical durability of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC and SVMG@Pd-SC devices. After 1000 bending cycles, the capacitance retentions were 92% and 85.4% for the SVMG + P@Pd-SC and SVMG@Pd-SC devices, respectively. Overall, these results provide compelling evidence for the robust mechanical properties of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device, confirming its sustainability for wearable applications requiring frequent mechanical deformations. Considering the device working in harsh environments, an investigation of the anti-leaking and anti-heating performance of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device was carried out by CV and GCD measurements operated under heated water at two different temperatures: 40 and 60 ºC. Figure S4a shows the CVs corresponding to the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device under heated water at 40 C (black curve) and 60 C (red curve). As shown, both CVs remained unchanged in shape with pseudocapacitive profile and nearly overlap, which should be due to the fact that the device remains isolated from water and maintains good internal stability of electron/ion conductivity at high temperatures. Moreover, Figure S4b shows that both GCDs have extended discharge time ending at supply voltages near to those obtained before immersing the device at heated water. The difference between the supply voltage of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC before and after immersing under heated water at 60 ºC (red curve) was only of 0.06 V. Thus, when using the red GCD curve to calculate the electrochemical performance, the capacitance and energy density of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device under heated water at 60 ºC reached values of 802.13 F g −1  and 109.42 Wh kg −1 , representing a 4.8% degradation of the supercapacitor when it is operated in a harsh environment. This low degradation indicates that the supercapacitor is physically and electrochemically stable for operation in electronics intended to work under water and at high temperatures. To gain deeper insight into the overall performance of the SCs, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) experiments were conducted on all the devices mentioned in the electrochemical performance results presented above (Gph-SC, SVMG-SC, SVMG@Pd-SC, SVMG + P@Pd-SC, and Gph + P@Pd-SC devices). The obtained EIS data are given in Nyquist plots, which are primary constituted by an impedance response as a function of frequency sweep going from low to high levels. In the high frequency region, the impedance curve intercepts the x-axis and gives valuable understanding about the series resistance (Rs) of the SC system, comprising contact resistance, solution resistance, and Intrinsic resistance of the working electrode [ 49 ]. Additionally, the charge transfer resistance (Rct) of the SC system can be also obtained from the high frequency region of the impedance curves. The value of the Rct, also known as the faradic resistance, indicates how efficiently charge is transferred through the electrode/electrolyte interface [ 49 ]. The equivalent circuit to match the EIS data by considering several elements including the Rs, Rct, and Warburg impedance (W) is illustrated in the inset of Fig.  7 a, which also displays the different impedance behaviors obtained in this study. Fig. 7 a  Impedance curves (Nyquist) obtained from the electrochemically evaluated SCs (Gph-SC, SVMG-SC, SVMG@Pd-SC, SVMG + P@Pd-SC, and Gph + P@Pd devices).  b  Impedance curves of the SVMG@Pd-SC after bending 1000 times and the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device subjected to 1000 bending cycles and under water at 40 °C and 60 °C. Inset of Fig.  6 b contains a photograph showing how the device was bent

It is visible from the Fig.  7 a that the impedance curve of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device showed the lowest Rs/Rct of 8.3/1.2 compared to the SVMG@Pd-SC (10.6/3.8), SVMG-SC (10.8/4.1), Gph+P@Pd-SC (15.8/5.3) andGph-SC (23.3/11.7 Ω) devices, demonstrating enhanced electrical conductivity and smooth charge transport across the interface of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device. This is attributed to the excellent synergy between the highly conductive components (P-NPs and Gph) and highly redox active elements (SVMG and Pd-NPs), along with the good compatibility between electrode and electrolyte. Interestingly, the three impedance curves of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC, SVMG@Pd-SC, and SVMG-SC devices possessed a straight line in the low frequency region corresponding to the Warburg impedance [ 50 ]. This implies the superior capacitance performance of these working electrodes in the SC systems, as it was confirmed with the electrochemical results previously obtained. Figure  7 b shows a comparison between the impedance curves obtained from the SVMG + P@Pd-SC and SVMG@Pd-SC devices after bending 1000 times. Clearly, the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device shows lower Rs/Rct values of 14.7/5.1 Ω compared to the SVMG@Pd-SC device (51.4/25.3 Ω). In addition, this figure also displays the impedance curves of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device operated under heated water at 40 and 60 ºC. Both Nyquist nearly overlaps at the interception in the x-axis, producing almost similar Rs/Rct values of 25.8/9.4 Ω. These outcomes indicate the lower resistance of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device, which was relatively maintained even after extensive mechanical stress and performance under harsh environment; thereby, this device exhibited superior stability in its electrochemical performance.

Since the components of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode have never been used in previous current studies about SCs, the performance comparison of our SVMG + P@Pd-SC device with the current literature was done by including those investigations where the working electrode of these devices was based on any of the individual components (SVMG, Pd, and/or P-NPs). A summary of these investigations is displayed in Table  1 , which includes the following results for capacitance and energy density: SiOC/Bi 2 O 3  nanocomposite (500 F g −1 , 98.2 Wh kg −1  at 882.4 W kg −1 ) [ 11 ]; SiOC into Gr hybrid membrane (211 F g −1 , 86.8 Wh kg −1  at 600 W kg −1 ) [ 12 ]; SiC and N, S doped porous carbon nanosheets (181.4 F g −1 , 5.2 Wh kg −1  at 251 W kg −1 ) [ 51 ]; PANI on NiCo 2 O 4  porous nanoflakes (406 F g −1 , 60.60 Wh kg −1  at 2322 W kg −1 ) [ 15 ]; MCo 2 O 4  nanospheres on PPy nanoparticles (350 F g −1 , 70 Wh kg −1 ) [ 18 ]; PEDOT:PSS decorated 2D-VS 2  doped with Ni (41.8 F g −1 , 47 Wh kg −1  at 992.9 W kg −1 ) [ 52 ]; Pd doped La 0.8 Sr 0.2 Cu 0.7 Mn 0.3 O 3  perovskite oxide (113 F g −1 , 68.3 Wh kg −1  at 1000 W kg −1 ) [ 19 ]; and PPy-PdO modified MXene (136 F g −1 , 64.5 Wh kg −1  at 980.9 W kg −1 ) [ 53 ]. According to such previous results, none of the studies that investigated SVMG, P-, and/or Pd-based materials in SCs systems surpassed our highest reported capacitance and energy density values. Moreover, a comparison with previous published data above indicates that our best SVMG + P@Pd-SC device had 30–91% higher energy density. Additionally, the Ragone plot in Figure S5 of supporting information shows that our best SC delivered the highest energy density and the lowest power density compared to the devices previously reported, that is, most of previous reported devices delivered the energy quickly (see the points around 1000 W kg −1 ). In contrast, our device had a low power density of 16.37 W kg −1 . Furthermore, the previous investigations did not report long-term stability under mechanical stress (bending cycles), which is a valuable feature for flexible supercapacitors (our best device supported 1000 bending cycles and de capacitance decreased only ~ 8%). Finally, the use of recycled polyethylene as flexible substrate to print the graphene electrodes is an added value to our investigation, which has been scarcely reported in the literature.

sections.heading: Analysis of defect-related features on the surface of the SC electrodes
paragraphs: As it is well known, surface defects, especially those defect related, play an important role in the charge/discharge mechanisms for SCs since they serve as energy storage sites [ 54 ]. Thus, UV/Vis and Raman characterization of the electrodes were performed in order to find these structural imperfections. First, UV/Vis measurements were conducted on the electrodes incorporating i) only Gph, ii) Gph plus the binary SVMG@Pd compound, and iii) Gph plus the ternary SVMG + P@Pd composite. The absorbance spectra obtained from such measurements before and after the corresponding use of each electrode inside the SC are shown in Fig.  8 a, b, respectively. As previously reported, higher the intensity of the absorbance, higher the density of defects on the material. In both Fig. 8a, b, the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode has a higher density of defects compared with the remaining electrodes. However, the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode used in the SC exhibited a 62% increase in the absorbance intensity compared to the non-used SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode. This is consistent with the fact that during electrochemical cycling, current flow and electrolyte interaction through the working electrode promotes larger presence of surface modifications available as redox sites, whereas the defect-related features on the non-used SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode are attributed to a synergistic effect between all the components of the ternary SVMG + P@Pd composite, contributing to an increase in oxygen vacancy defects within the Gph structure [ 55 ,  56 ]. Fig. 8 UV/Vis absorbance spectra for the Gph-E, SVMG-E, SVMG@Pd-E, and SVMG + P@Pd-E electrodes:  a  not used in the SC and  b  utilized in the SC

Furthermore, as the wavelength increases through the visible region (400–750 nm), the spectra exhibit improvement in light absorption, which can be triggered by the induced surface defects as well [ 57 ]. To provide further insights into the defect’s density, the same electrodes (Gph-E, SVMG@Pd-E, and SVMG + P@Pd-E electrodes) were analyzed with the Raman technique.

Specifically, the Raman spectrum of carbon-based materials displays two significant bands: the D band (at ~ 1320 cm −1 ) arising from surface defects in the crystalline structure of carbon compounds such as edges, vacancies, and functional groups; and the G band (at ~ 1580 cm −1 ), which is intrinsically linked to the graphitic nature of carbon (sp 2 -bonded carbon configuration) [ 58 ,  59 ]. Thus, changes in the intensity ratio between these bands (I (D/G) ) acts as a reliable metric for quantifying the density of defects in the SC electrodes [ 60 ].

Figure  9 a displays that the Gph electrode presents an I (D/G)  ratio of 0.41, indicating that the graphene sheets have a high degree of graphitization with a low concentration of defects, which are primarily attributed to functional groups on the surface of the Gph oxide sheets introduced after electrode fabrication. Moreover, Fig.  9 b shows that after incorporating the SVMG powder on the Gph sheets in the SVMG-E, the I (D/G)  ratio increased ~ 1.1 times, reaching a value of 0.45. This occurred because intrinsic defects of the SVMG, such as edge defects and functionalized sites attached to the Gph layers. A similar effect was observed after incorporating the binary SVMG@Pd compound on the Gph layers. This time, the Raman spectrum of the SVMG@Pd-E electrode had an I (D/G)  ratio of 0.63, see Fig.  9 c. This ratio is ~ 1.5 times higher than the one obtained from the Gph-E but ~ 2.1 times lower than the I (D/G)  exhibited by the Raman spectrum of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode, which was 1.33, see Fig.  9 d. This result strongly suggests that the presence of the ternary SVMG + P@Pd composite is essential to increase the type of defects altering the chemical/electronic properties of Gph to a considerable level that allows superior number of active sites for the charge storage, resulting in the exceptional electrochemical performance from the device using the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode. Fig. 9 Raman spectra of electrodes:  a  Gph-E,  b  SVMG-E,  c  SVMG@Pd-E, and  d  SVMG + P@Pd-E

sections.heading: XPS characterization to determine the energy storage mechanism the SCs
paragraphs: Due to the presence of redox compounds in the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode, such as SVMG and Pd, which contain oxygen vacancies and mixed oxidation states, this electrode clearly exhibited redox activity during electrochemical cycling (refer to the CVs of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device). Therefore, XPS measurements were recorded on the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode to reveal the chemical states of the species present in the electrode before and after its electrochemical cycling (use in the SC). Figure  10 a depicts the XPS spectrum for the O 1 s orbital and corresponds to the non-used SC electrode. Fig. 10 XPS spectra recorded for the SVMG + P@Pd-E before and after its use in the SC:  a / b  O 1 s orbital,  c / d  Si 2p orbital, and  e / f  Pd 3d orbital

The single band is deconvoluted with three peaks located at 530.7 (O a ), 531.5 (O b ), and 532.2 eV (O c ), where O a  and O c  are related to Mn/V–O and PdO 2  bonds, while O b  is ascribed to oxygen vacancy defects, confirming the existence of the Mn/V and P-based oxide phases and native defects on the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode, which were also detected and measured by FTIR, UV/Vis, and Raman techniques in previous sections [ 61 ,  62 ]. Then, the XPS for the O1s was recorded and deconvoluted again, but now after the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode was extracted from the tested SC. This new spectrum displays the O b  and O c  peaks, along with new ones indicative of the oxidation of graphene’s surface: O = C bond at 531.8 eV and C-O bond at 532.9 eV; and another peak corresponding to adsorbed OH groups (O h ) forming new species of hydroxides (Metal-OH, O–H, etc.) [ 63 ,  64 ]. Comparing the O b  peaks of Fig.  10 a, b, it is revealed a clear decrease in the area of the peak after electrochemical cycling, which could indicate fewer presence of OVs on the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode during operation on the SC. However, adsorbed oxygen species like O = C, C-O, and O–H are commonly associated with the generation of surface oxygen vacancies, indicating an enhancement of these kind of defects after the use of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode in the SC and in consequence, the boost of charge storage by redox reactions [ 65 ]. Additionally, Fig.  10 c, d present the deconvoluted peaks for the XPS spectrum of the Si 2p orbital before and after the use of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode in the SC, respectively. Figure  10 c illustrates five peaks corresponding to three different oxidation states of Si-related oxide products (SiO, Si 2 O 3  and SiO 2 ): Si 2+ , Si 3+ , and Si 4+  [ 66 ]. In contrast, Fig.  10 d depicts only two deconvoluted peaks from the single band of the Si 2p orbital. Both peaks, which are located at 103.7 and 104.2 eV, correspond to the Si 4+  of SiO 2  and Si-O 4 , respectively [ 66 ,  67 ]. Clearly, the content of Si 4+  increased in the electrode used in the SC, confirming the redox reaction for the Si species. Furthermore, the disappearance of the Si 2+  and Si 3+  from this last XPS analysis indicates that both are completely transformed to Si 4+  during the electrochemical cycling of the electrode. On the other hand, the XPS spectrum of the Pd 3d orbital was also analyzed for the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode (not used in the SC), see Fig.  10 e. This spectrum presents peaks at 334.7–335.8 eV and 339.7–340.8 eV, which correspond to the doublet Pd 3d 5/2  and Pd 3d 3/2 , respectively, indicating the presence of Pd nanoparticles in the zero (0) oxidation state [ 68 ]. Also, the deconvoluted peak at 338.1 eV corresponds to the most oxidized state of Pd (4 +) and it could be attributed to the PdO phase established in the synthesis of the Pd nanoparticles [ 69 ]. Next, the same spectrum was re-analyzed after removing the used electrode from the SC, see Fig.  10 f. This time, the position of the Pd 3d 5/2  and Pd 3d 3/2  peaks did not substantially varying, reflecting the presence of the Pd 0  oxidation state. However, new Pd 2+  species appear, which were not previously observed, with one peak centered at 336.1 eV [ 70 ]. Furthermore, the presence of the Pd 4+  species is now reflected with peak at 343.3 eV [ 71 ]. Such changes in the XPS spectrum indicate that Pd 4+  species were converted to Pd 2+ , confirming the redox reaction of Pd nanoparticles into the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode during SC operation. On the other hand, XPS spectra for Mn 2p and V 2p orbitals were also obtained from the unused SVMG + P@Pd-E and they are separately displayed in Figure S6a and S6b, respectively. Figure S6a depicts the Mn 2p spectrum deconvoluted to Mn 2+  (at 640.8 and 641.8 eV), Mn 3+  (at 643.2 and 63.1 eV), and Mn 4+  with a satellite peak at 646.5 eV [ 72 ]. This results indicate the formation of Mn 3 O 4  with oxide compositions of MnO 2  and MnO on the structure of the SVMG [ 73 ]. In the case of the V 2p orbital, the deconvolution of the spectrum of Figure S6b indicates that the oxidation sates of V in the SVMG compound are 3 + (515.5 eV), 4 + (516.5 and 523.4 eV) and 5 + (517.5 and 524.7 eV), which confirms the presence of VO 2 , as well as a small amount of V 2 O 5  and V 2 O 3  on the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode [ 74 ]. According to previous reports, the presence of this mixture of Mn and V-based oxides on the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode is particularly important for SC performance because their stoichiometrically components can be transform during electrochemical cycling. For example, Mn 3+  and Mn 2+  can be transformed to Mn 4+  and Mn 3+ /Mn 4+  components, respectively, while V 5+ /V 4+  couple can be transformed to V 3+ /V 4+  [ 75 ,  76 ]. This changes in the oxidation state of Mn/V-based oxides indicates redox activity occurring on the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode to store charge after the adsorption of electrolyte ions. Overall, the results for XPS indicate that among all the components in the SVMG + P@Pd-E, SVMG (with Si 2+ /Si 3+ /Si 4+ , Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ / Mn 4+  and V 3+ /V 4+ /V 5+  species), and Pd (with Pd 2+ /Pd 4+  species) are the ones participating in the redox generation of electrons, which can be then captured (reduction reaction) or released (oxidation reaction) by oxygen vacancies also formed on the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode. On the other hand, it is important to mention that the results of electrochemical performance for the SVMG-SC, Gph + Pd-SC, and SVMG + P@Pd-SC devices were compared in order to see the impact of each redox species in the performance behavior. The capacitance of each device can be order as follows: 828.3 F g −1  (SVMG + P@Pd-SC) > 492.90 F g −1  (SVMG-SC) > 436.43 F g −1  (Gph + Pd-SC). As observed, the capacitance of the Gph + Pd-SC (containing only the Pd 2+ /Pd 4+  species) was 11% lower than the one of the SVMG-SC (containing multiple Si 2+ /Si 3+ /Si 4+ , Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ / Mn 4+ , and V 3+ /V 4+ /V 5+  species). In addition, the capacitance of the Gph + Pd-SC and SVMG-SC devices was 47% and 40% lower than that for the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device (containing all the Pd 2+ /Pd 4+ , Si 2+ /Si 3+ /Si 4+ , Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ / Mn 4+ , and V 3+ /V 4+ /V 5+  species). Hence, it is inferred that the sum of all the redox species, Pd 2+ /Pd 4+ , Si 2+ /Si 3+ /Si 4+ , Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ / Mn 4+ , and V 3+ /V 4+ /V 5+ , caused higher storage of charge in the supercapacitor.

sections.heading: Photocatalytic activity of the SVMG + P@Pd-E composite and its working mechanism
paragraphs: The excellent synergy between the components of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode, which include the presence of various metal oxides (confirmed with XPS analysis), Pd-NPs, and Gph, suggests the use of such electrode as photocatalytic floater for the degradation of MB (dissolved in drinking water) under sunlight. This is because metal oxides can photogenerate charge for photocatalytic activity, while Pd-NPs and Gph can enhance the photocatalytic activity by delaying the recombination rates of photogenerated charge carriers. Thus, the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode is now re-named as SVMG + P@Pd–PT composite for the photocatalytic experiments. The photocatalytic activity of SVMG + P@Pd–PT was subsequently compared with these for other photocatalytic composites such as graphene + SVMG (SVMG-PT) or graphene + SVMG@Pd (SVMG@Pd–PT). The results of the photocatalytic degradation for MB as a function of time (t) are displayed in Fig.  11 a. After 120 min, the maximum degradation percentages of the dye were 89%, 85%, and 84% for the SVMG + P@Pd–PT, SVMG@Pd, and SVMG-PT, respectively. In fact, the SVMG + P@Pd–PT composite produced the faster photocatalytic degradation for MB dye. This composite produced 80% degradation of MB after only 30 min of sunlight irradiation. Continuous cycles of reuse were also performed for the degradation of MB by using the best the SVMG + P@Pd–PT composite and the efficiency decreased from 89 to 82% after 3 cycles of use. Thus, the MB degradation efficiency decreased by 7.8% after using 3 times continuously the SVMG + P@Pd–PT composite. Fig. 11 MB degradation curves using  a  SVMG-PT, SVMG@Pd–PT, SVMG + P@Pd–PT composites and  b  different scavengers (BZ, TA, and KI) as well as SVMG + P@Pd–PT under sunlight exposure

Since the degradation percentage was enhanced by 5.9% (compared to the SVMG-PT) after adding together all the components (SVMG, P-, and Pd-NPs) to the Gph-based photocatalyst, it is proper to highlight the importance of the high concentration of surface defects and Pd in the SVMG + P@Pd–PT, which amplify the absorption of light in the visible spectrum range, delay the recombination of charge carriers, and enhance the photocatalytic activity of SVMG, promoting decomposition of MB molecules. Particularly, oxygen vacancy defects are highly relevant herein because they work as trapping centers for electrons and delay their recombination, favoring the photocatalytic process. To emphasize the significance of the best degradation percentage for our photocatalyst floater composite SVMG + P@Pd (89%), a comparative analysis was undertaken. Table  2  provides shows the photocatalytic parameters for photocatalysts reported in recent literature, which contains Gph, SVMG, P-, and/or Pd-NPs. For example, one investigation involving Pd loaded bismuth ferrite nanoparticles (BFO), and other using a Pd/Au decorated reduced graphene oxide (rGO) nanocomposite for the dye degradation of MG and RhB, respectively. In the first case, a maximum dye degradation efficiency of 51% was obtained after 1 h exposure time under sunlight, while for the second case, the photocatalytic achieved an impressive 98% degradation efficiency by using the same conditions: 1 h exposure time at direct sunlight illumination [ 20 ,  22 ]. Also, the use of Gr, in the form of graphene oxide, for the dye degradation has been documented with maximum efficiencies of 80% in 2 h (for methyl orange under sunlight) and 90% in 90 min (for MB under UV-A light) [ 77 ,  78 ]. Furthermore, the impact of conductive polymers like PPy and PANI has been investigated toward photocatalytic degradation of dyes such as MB and Thymol blue. For MB, the PPy-based composite (PPy/Cu doped ZnO) exhibited a maximum degradation of 92% in 210 min of direct sunlight exposure, whereas thymol blue was photodegraded 96% after irradiation of visible light (provided by Hanovia lamp) for 3 h [ 79 ,  80 ]. Furthermore, composites of SiC (PMo 12 /SiC and Ag 3 /TiO 2 /regenerated SiC) have been used for the removal of MG and RhB under the irradiation of visible light (provided by different types of lamps) with efficiencies of 95% within 2 h and 99.3% within 15 min, respectively [ 81 ,  82 ]. It is noticeable that, excluding references [ 20 ] and [ 77 ], the remained studies produced a higher dye degradation than our SVMG + P@Pd–PT composite. Thus, further research needs to be conducted to address the following limitations of our system: i) Photocatalyst concentration in the contaminated water: A high content of photocatalyst in the contaminated water could lead to a diminution of degradation efficiency for the MB contaminant. This decrease of efficiency occurred due to photocatalyst aggregation, which limits the amount of MB adsorbed on the photocatalyst surface and restricts the absorption of light; thus, it is necessary an optimization to find the optimum concentration of photocatalyst for our system. ii) MB dye concentration: the photocatalytic degradation efficiency could increase by decreasing the concentration of MB dye to similar concentrations previously reported (10 ppm). iii) Ratio between Pd-NPs and Polymeric-NPs: As demonstrated above, the efficiency of the photocatalyst drastically increases after the aggregation of the Pd-NPs and Polymeric-NPs. However, we did not study how the Pd-NPs/Polymeric-NPs ratio affects the degradation of MB dye; thus, it is necessary more studies to find the optimum Pd-NPs/Polymeric-NPs ratio, which maximizes the degradation of MB dye. Although we had MB degradation efficiency slightly lower (89%) in comparison with some previous systems (> 95%), still the best SVMG + P@Pd–PT photocatalyst studied in this work presents the following significant advantages: i) high absorption of light in the visible region, see Fig.  8 , which promotes the photocatalysis process and the degradation of dyes; ii) easy recovery from clean water: The SVMG + P@Pd–PT composite is easily placed and recovered from the contaminated/clean water, since it remains floating during the degradation of MB dye, which is not possible using the photocatalytic powders previously reported in the literature, since they remained suspended in the clean water after dye degradation, and be removed using only complex centrifugation methods; iii) it contains the SVMG powder, which has a high content of vacancy defects, which promote the degradation of MB dye.

On the other hand, the identification of the main oxidizing species released by the SVMG + P@Pd–PT composite under sunlight and understanding of the removal mechanism for MB was achieved through scavengers experiments. For this purpose, the BZ, KI, and TA compounds were utilized as quenchers to detect superoxide anions (•O 2 − ), holes (h + ) and hydroxyl radicals (•OH), respectively [ 83 ,  84 ]. In this experiment, an analogous methodology to that used in Sect.  2.6  was employed, with the addition of 1 mmol of trapping reagents (scavengers) in the presence of MB dye and SVMG + P@Pd photocatalyst. Based on the degradation vs. time results displayed in Fig.  11 b, the percentages of MB degradation at t = 180 min can be ordered as follows: TA (99.8%) > BZ (97.3%) > KI (77.5%). This means that holes were the dominant oxidizing species produced for the photocatalytic degradation of MB, while the radicals •O 2 −  and •OH were the secondary oxidizing agents. Thus the following reactions are proposed for the formation of these oxidizing agents by solar photocatalysis:

A proposed schematic illustration for photocatalytic reactions (Eqs. 4–8) is designed for MB degradation in Figure S7. Initially, the SVMG + P@Pd compound of the photocatalyst is irradiated with sunlight, producing the electron (e − )–hole (h + ) pair in the conduction band (cb) and valence band (vb), respectively. When Pd is in contact with the polymeric nanoparticles and the SVMG microparticles in the photocatalytic composite, it creates a Schottky barrier. The difference in their work function causes electrons to flow from the polymer layer into the Pd [ 85 ]. Then, Pd acts as an efficient electron sink in the compound [ 86 ]. By trapping photogenerated electrons from the polymer’s conduction band at these metallic sites, Pd drastically extends the lifetime of the photoinduced charge carriers, making them available for redox reactions with the water molecules, which in turn, produce the oxidizing agents responsible for the degradation of MB dye. Furthermore, Pd provides active sites where the trapped electrons can directly produce reduction reactions with lower energy barriers. Additionally, the porous morphology of the polymeric layer (see Fig.  1 c) helps water percolate better through the composite, which enhanced the adsorption of MB on the active material and benefits the photocatalytic process for the degradation of MB dye [ 85 ,  86 – 87 ]. Once these charge carriers have been photogenerated, they are transported to the surface Ov and Gph. From here, the photogenerated electrons can react with the oxygen adsorbed in the surface of the photocatalyst, leading to the generation of •O 2 −  radicals. Similarly, holes interact with the elements in the polluted water (H 2 O) to form •OH radicals. Finally, these radicals react with the MB molecule, initiating dye degradation into smaller and non-toxic compounds. This mechanism highlights the importance of the surface defects on the Gph substrate containing the highly photosensitive SVMG + P@Pd compound since they significantly delay the recombination of photogenerated charge carries, which increase the generation of •O 2 −  radicals and the presence of holes, facilitating the MB degradation.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Along with Gph, synthesized SVMG powders, P- and Pd-NPs particles were successfully employed for the fabrication of SCs and the degradation of MB. For this, Gph layers printed on recycled PP substrates served as highly conductive substrate on which a SVMG + P@Pd composite was introduced, serving in this way as both SC electrode and photocatalytic floater. The application of the SVMG + P@Pd as electrode, allowed the fabrication of an asymmetric SC (SVMG + P@Pd-SC) that displayed superior capacitance of 828.3 F g −1  and energy density of 115.03 Wh kg −1 . The synergy between each component of the SVMG + P@Pd-E electrode was proved to be highly important in the obtention of such outstanding electrochemical performance since the exclusion of one, two, or more components lowered the capacitance and energy density values obtained from the SC by up to 40%. For example, SCs made only with Gph electrodes (Gph-SC) and Gph layer incorporating SVMG (SVMG-SC), SVMG@Pd (SVMG@Pd-SC), and P@Pd (Gph + P@Pd-SC) exhibited capacitance/energy density values of 428.47 F g −1 /59.51 Wh kg −1 , 492.90 F g −1 /68.45 Wh kg −1 , 507.74 F g −1 /70.52 Wh kg −1 , and 432.21 F g −1 /65.78 Wh kg −1 , respectively. Additionally, the SVMG + P@Pd-SC showed to be robust enough to support mechanical stress and extended cycling with above 90% of capacitance retention after the application 1000 charge/discharge and 1000 bending cycles, respectively. Even more, this device was subjected to immersion at heated water (with a maximum temperature of 60 °C) and its overall performance only decreased by 4.8%, suggesting great anti-leaking and anti-heating performance. Various species, including Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ / Mn 4+ , V 3+ /V 4+ /V 5+  Si 2+ /Si 3+ /Si 4+ , Pd 2+ /Pd 4+ , and oxygen vacancies, were identified (through UV/Vis, Raman, and XPS) to be the primary centers responsible for the outstanding performance of the SVMG + P@Pd-SC device. On the other hand, the SVMG + P@Pd composite used as photocatalytic floater achieved 89% MB degradation after 30 min of sunlight exposure. This result, which showed to be comparatively high to other studies in recent literature, was obtained due to several factors, including the presence of Pd-NPs, surface vacancies and Gph in the composition of the photocatalyst. This is because these components proved to delay the recombination of the photoinduced electrons and holes, which were the dominant reactive species for MB degradation. Such findings, along with flexibility, low cost, and floatability, make the SVMG + P@Pd composite good candidate for its use in water treatment and energy storage applications.
